content: This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review that aims to evaluate the effects of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation on depression in children and adolescents aged 6 to 19 years. The review will compare omega-3 PUFA supplementation to a placebo or other control groups, such as wait-list controls, to assess its impact on both clinician-diagnosed depression and self-reported depressive symptoms. The review will also estimate the magnitude of the effect of omega-3 PUFAs on depression and evaluate the specific effects of different types of omega-3 PUFAs, such as eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), compared to placebo. Additionally, it will investigate whether the effects of omega-3 PUFAs are influenced by factors such as dosage, delivery format (e.g., capsules or liquid), sex, or age. Mental health disorders, including depression, often begin during childhood or adolescence. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), nearly 20% of children and adolescents worldwide experience mental health disorders, with depression and anxiety being the most common. Depression typically emerges after puberty, with prevalence increasing around the age of 10, particularly in girls. Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and dysthymia are two common types of unipolar depressive disorders in this age group. MDD is characterized by a persistently low mood, irritability, or loss of interest in activities for at least two weeks, while dysthymia involves less severe but more chronic symptoms lasting at least one year. Children and adolescents with depression may also experience changes in energy levels, appetite, sleep patterns, restlessness, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, hopelessness, indecisiveness, or thoughts of self-harm or suicide. The diagnostic criteria for depression in children and adolescents are similar to those for adults, although irritability may replace sadness as a primary symptom in younger individuals. Current treatment options for childhood and adolescent depression include pharmacological, psychological, and combined approaches. However, poor response rates to existing treatments and high rates of relapse highlight the need for alternative therapies. Omega-3 PUFAs, which are naturally found in fatty fish, marine sources, and some nuts and seeds, have emerged as a potential treatment for depression. Systematic reviews have shown that omega-3 PUFAs are effective in treating MDD in adults, although the quality of evidence remains uncertain. The beneficial effects of omega-3 PUFAs are thought to depend on factors such as dosage and the specific type of omega-3 fatty acid used. Omega-3 PUFAs are essential fatty acids that cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be obtained through diet. The three main types of omega-3 fatty acids are alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), EPA, and DHA. ALA is found in plant-based sources such as flaxseed, walnuts, and hemp, while EPA and DHA are primarily found in oily fish like salmon, mackerel, and sardines. ALA can be converted into EPA and DHA in the body, but this process is highly inefficient, with only 1% to 15% of ALA being metabolized. Dietary supplements containing EPA and DHA are considered the most effective way to increase levels of these fatty acids in the body. Observational studies have linked fish oil, which contains both EPA and DHA, to a reduced risk of depression. The International Society for Nutritional Psychiatry Research (ISNPR) recommends omega-3 PUFA supplementation as a preventive treatment for depression in high-risk adult populations, and the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments (CANMAT) suggests omega-3 PUFAs as a second-line monotherapy for mild to moderate MDD or as an adjunctive treatment for moderate to severe MDD in adults. However, no guidelines currently exist for children and adolescents. Omega-3 PUFAs are believed to exert their antidepressant effects through multiple mechanisms. They are essential for brain function and development, particularly during puberty, when processes such as myelination and synaptic pruning occur. Omega-3 PUFAs are integral components of neuronal cell membranes, where they influence membrane fluidity and integrity, which in turn affects neurotransmission. DHA, in particular, plays a critical role in maintaining cell membrane flexibility, which facilitates the transmission of signals between neurons. Omega-3 PUFAs also impact the activity of membrane-bound enzymes, receptors, and ion channels, as well as the production and activity of neurotransmitters. Additionally, they influence neuroplasticity and the expression of neurotrophins such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which supports neuronal growth and function. Omega-3 PUFAs also have anti-inflammatory properties, which may contribute to their antidepressant effects. High levels of inflammation have been associated with the progression and severity of depression. Chronic stress can activate the immune system, leading to a neuroinflammatory response and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α). These inflammatory mediators can disrupt neurotransmitter activity and contribute to depressive symptoms. Omega-3 PUFAs have been shown to reduce the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and increase the release of anti-inflammatory mediators, such as eicosanoids and prostaglandins. They also enhance serotonergic and dopaminergic activity while reducing noradrenaline concentrations, which may further alleviate depressive symptoms. Despite the growing evidence supporting the use of omega-3 PUFAs for depression in adults, there is limited research on their efficacy in children and adolescents. This review aims to address this gap by synthesizing and quantifying the current evidence on omega-3 PUFA supplementation for depression in this population. Providing high-quality evidence on the effectiveness of omega-3 PUFAs as an alternative or adjunctive therapy for depression in children and adolescents is crucial for informing clinical practice and developing dietary guidelines.
